Different kinds of manufacturing. The same data problems, in different forms.

A semiconductor fab, a machine shop, and a process plant do not run the same operation, and nobody should pretend they do. What they share is quieter than that: production numbers that live in more than one system, definitions that were never written down, and reports that disagree with each other in front of the people who have to act on them. Prime works across manufacturing because that underlying problem is the same work everywhere it shows up, and it has to be understood in the terms of the plant in front of us before anything is built on top of it.

Industries

Where the work applies, stated plainly

Each section below says what that kind of operation needs, what usually goes wrong with its numbers, and what Prime can provide there. Where our background is direct, the section says so. Where a kind of manufacturing is a fit for the same work rather than a place we have already worked, the section says that instead, because the difference matters and we would rather state it than blur it.

Direct experience

Semiconductor and electronics manufacturing

This is where our manufacturing background was earned. Antonio Rojas spent 18 years inside Semtech’s semiconductor manufacturing operations as Sr. Manager and Manager of Applications Development, responsible for the enterprise applications the operation ran on, so the needs below are described from having carried them, not from reading about them.

What this operation needs

A fab or an electronics plant needs its MES, its ERP, and its test and yield data to tell one consistent story about a lot as it moves, because decisions about holds, rework, and shipment get made on those numbers while the product is still moving, and a number nobody can trace back to its source is a number nobody should act on.

What usually goes wrong

Yield is the number that argues back. Operations calculates it one way, finance another, and the export that runs overnight can disagree with the MES screen the floor is looking at, so the same question gets two defensible answers and the meeting becomes about the arithmetic instead of the product.

What Prime can provide

A diagnostic that maps how lot, yield, and inventory data actually moves between the MES and the ERP, written down in definitions your own engineers can challenge, followed by an architecture and a small pilot in your own systems before anyone commits to a larger build.

Experience, in the ERP layer

Discrete manufacturing: machining, fabrication, and equipment

Our experience here is real but narrow, and we state it narrowly: it sits in the ERP layer these plants run on, not inside a machining or fabrication plant of our own. Antonio’s work with MAPICS, now Infor XA, covered the parts of that ERP that discrete manufacturers live in every day: bills of materials, inventory, and shop activity, across operations in the United States and Mexico. We are not claiming to have run your shop floor, and the distinction is stated because it is real.

What this operation needs

A job shop or a fabrication plant needs the bill of materials, the routing, and the inventory count to agree with what is physically on the floor, because quoting, scheduling, and purchasing all read from those records, and a BOM that drifted away from how the part is actually built quietly taxes every job that runs through it.

What usually goes wrong

The ERP says one quantity, the shelf holds another, and the spreadsheet someone maintains by hand holds a third. Shop activity gets reported at the end of the shift instead of as it happens, so the schedule is always describing yesterday, and nobody can say exactly when the records stopped matching the floor.

What Prime can provide

A diagnostic that follows one part or one job from quote to shipment and writes down where the records diverge, then a scoped pilot, for example around inventory accuracy or shop reporting, built inside the ERP and spreadsheets you already use rather than a replacement platform.

Where this applies

Process manufacturing: chemicals, materials, food and beverage

We have not run applications inside a process plant, and this section does not claim otherwise. It is here because the shape of the data problem is one we know well: batch records, formulas, and quality results that have to agree across systems that were never designed to agree, in an operation where the product cannot be unmade when the numbers turn out to be wrong.

What this operation needs

A process operation needs batch and lot traceability that holds up end to end, from raw material intake through the run to the shipped product, with formula versions, yields, and quality results recorded the same way every time, because when a customer or a regulator asks what went into a batch, the answer has to be a record and not a reconstruction.

What usually goes wrong

The batch record lives in one system, the lab results in another, and the ERP holds a yield figure that neither of them produced. Material loss gets explained differently by production and by finance, and the explanation that survives is usually the one belonging to whoever wrote the report, not the one the data supports.

What Prime can provide

The same diagnostic discipline we apply in discrete and semiconductor work: pick one product family or one recurring argument about yield or loss, document how the numbers are produced today across the batch record, the lab, and the ERP, and write down the definitions before any analytics or AI is pointed at them.

Where this applies

Assembly and high mix production

Contract manufacturers, electronics assemblers, and plants running many products through shared lines face a version of the same problem at higher speed. This is a fit for our work rather than a setting we describe from the inside, and it is included because the failure pattern, three systems describing the same order three different ways, is exactly the kind of handoff a diagnostic exists to trace: follow the order from the promise to the build to the shipment, and write down where the three accounts of it stop matching.

What this operation needs

A high mix operation needs the order promise made in the CRM, the build recorded in the MES, and the shipment and invoice in the ERP to describe the same job, because changeovers, short runs, and customer changes punish any gap between what sales committed and what the floor was told, and the gap usually surfaces at the dock.

What usually goes wrong

The customer change lands in email or in the CRM and never reaches the build record, work in progress is counted differently by the line and by accounting, and the status a customer is given on the phone comes from whichever system the person answering happened to open first.

What Prime can provide

A diagnostic focused on one order flow, from quote to shipment, that writes down where the CRM, the MES, and the ERP stop agreeing and who owns each handoff, followed by a pilot that connects one of those handoffs properly before anyone talks about automating the rest.

Where this applies

Regulated manufacturing: medical devices and aerospace suppliers

Regulated operations are a fit for this work because documentation is not overhead there, it is the product’s license to ship. Our semiconductor background sits in an industry with its own strict quality and traceability demands, which is relevant experience, but we do not present it as medical device or aerospace work, and any engagement here starts by learning your regulatory frame from the people accountable for it.

What this operation needs

A regulated plant needs device history, inspection results, and corrective actions to form one traceable record that an auditor can follow without help, and it needs every definition that feeds that record, from acceptance criteria to scrap classification, to be written down and owned by a named person rather than carried as habit.

What usually goes wrong

The quality system says one thing, the MES records another, and the ERP closes the order on a third understanding of what passed. The records are usually complete in the sense that every field is filled in, and inconsistent in the sense that matters, which only becomes visible when an audit or a complaint forces the three to be read side by side.

What Prime can provide

A diagnostic that reads your operation the way an auditor would, following one product’s record across the quality system, the MES, and the ERP, and writing down every place the story changes. Any build that follows stays inside your validated systems, and our recommendations do not replace review by your own quality and regulatory owners.

Applications

The same three systems, in every industry above

Whatever the product, the argument is usually between the same three systems of record. The MES knows what the floor did, the ERP knows what the business recorded, and the CRM knows what the customer was told, and AI applied to any one of them inherits whatever disagreement was already there.

AI for MES

Your MES holds the operational record: lots, batches, work in progress, and the events of the shift. Before a model answers questions about it, the meaning of its fields and the way your floor actually uses them has to be written down, because a 400 table database does not explain itself and a plausible answer built on the wrong table is worse than no answer.

AI for ERP

The ERP holds the business record: bills of materials, inventory, orders, and cost. Its numbers are only as good as the definitions and the discipline behind them, so the work starts by establishing which figures the business will stand behind, and only then deciding what a model may read, summarize, or act on.

AI for CRM

The CRM holds what the customer heard: quotes, promises, changes, and complaints. Automation touches customers directly, so the context behind a commitment has to be clear before anything is automated, and the record of what was promised has to stay reconcilable with what the plant can actually build.

Diagnostics

Every industry starts the same way: with a diagnostic

The first step does not change with the industry, because the risk is the same in all of them: building on top of numbers nobody has verified. We start by documenting your operation as it actually runs, in your own systems, and the written record is yours to keep and to challenge whether or not any build follows from it.

1

Diagnostic

We sit with the floor team and the people who own the numbers, pick one decision the plant needs to get right, and trace how it is made today, system by system and handoff by handoff.

2

Write it down

The definitions, the calculations, the exceptions, and the owners go into a written record your team can inspect and argue with, because an argument about a written definition is how the record gets better.

3

Architecture and pilot

From the written record we design a small pilot around that one decision, scoped tightly enough that its result can be judged honestly, including the honest result that a build is not worth doing.

4

Implementation support

If the pilot earns it, we support the implementation inside the systems you already run, and the final decisions about access, scope, and what gets built and used stay with you and your own owners throughout.

What Prime can provide, across industries

  • Documentation of how MES, ERP, and CRM data actually moves through your operation
  • Written definitions for the numbers your plant argues about, with a named owner for each one
  • Mapping of undocumented databases and application logic into a record engineers can use
  • Analytics and dashboards built on definitions that have been agreed in writing first
  • Architecture for AI and analytics work that stays inside your own systems
  • Pilot design, and implementation support once a pilot has been judged worth scaling

Insights

What we keep seeing, in plant after plant

The data is rarely missing

Most plants we look at already collect more data than anyone reads. What is missing is an agreed account of what the data means, and that is a writing problem before it is a technology problem, which is why it survives every new tool purchase.

The spreadsheet is a symptom

When a careful person maintains a private spreadsheet that half the plant quietly depends on, they are telling you exactly where the official systems stopped being trusted, and that spreadsheet is usually the most honest map of the real process available anywhere.

Definitions differ because jobs differ

Operations and finance define yield differently because they are answering different questions, and neither is wrong. The failure is not the difference, it is that the difference was never written down, so each side believes the other has made an error.
